blocks.raw:
<Tip>**Internal forces — five types remembered by location and effect:**
- **Tension & Compression = axial** (along the member length; pulling or pushing)
- **Shear = transverse** (perpendicular; sliding)
- **Bending = moment** (curves the member)
- **Torsion = twisting moment** (rotates about the axis)

**Shear is highest at supports; bending is highest at midspan (for simply supported beams).**</Tip>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Treating bending and shear as the same thing: Shear is a transverse force; bending is a moment. They are related (shear causes bending to vary) but distinct. A beam can have shear with zero moment at one section and moment with zero shear at another.","Confusing torsion with bending: Torsion twists the member about its axis; bending curves it perpendicular to the axis. A twisted beam and a bent beam have opposite failure modes.","Assuming all axial force is tension: Compression is equally important; columns are critical structural elements that must be designed for compressive strength and buckling resistance. Compression is not a weakness; it is a load type.","Forgetting that tension cannot reverse in some materials: Concrete and masonry have low or zero tensile strength. A structural element that experiences tension in concrete design requires reinforcement; plain concrete cannot carry tension alone.","Ignoring shear in design: Shear forces create diagonal cracks in concrete and grain splitting in timber. Shear must be checked; it is not a secondary effect."]} />
